title: AI-assisted browser puzzle devlog: I separated beam visibility from what actually lets the walker move
author: Western-Principle639
selftext:
I’m developing Alley Light, a small puzzle game where a traveler waits for the next lit step. I used Codex to help build the Three.js game logic and procedural scene code. A recurring problem was a beam that looked plausible in the scene while the step check gave a different answer. Breaking the behavior into explicit tests for occlusion, reflection and the next step gave me smaller things to verify in an actual run.

The recent night market rework was a good test. A lantern has to be illuminated before the second lamp powers on. I could check the lantern activation, how the cable indicates the power connection, and the walker’s next step separately. Playtest feedback also led me to give rotation and sliding different controls on the lamp itself.

I’d be interested in how others keep visual feedback and rule checks in sync in AI-assisted game builds. [Free desktop browser demo](https://jackyrl0218.itch.io/alley-light-playtest).

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body: same problem here, except our visual side is an LLM narrator instead of a renderer. what kept them in sync was ordering. the model can only ask for an action through a tool call, the rules code resolves it and hands back the result, and only then does it describe anything, so it can't show a hit that didn't happen

replies.author: Western-Principle639
replies.body: Resolving the action before the narrator describes it makes a lot of sense. I can use that same ordering here: resolve whether the beam reaches the next step or gets blocked, then use that result for both the on-screen feedback and the walker. Shutters and mirrors are where that matters most. Thanks for sharing how you handled it.
